title: Isomorphic Strings
directAnswer: Two strings are isomorphic if there is a consistent one-to-one (bijective) character mapping from s to t that preserves order. The canonical answer scans both strings together and enforces the mapping in BOTH directions: s→t must be consistent AND t→s must be consistent. One map is not enough — you need two maps (or a map plus a reverse-membership set). O(n) time, O(1) space (fixed alphabet).

remember.pattern: Bijection check with two maps (forward + reverse)
remember.formula:
for (a, b) in zip(s, t):
    if a in mapST and mapST[a] != b: return False
    if b in mapTS and mapTS[b] != a: return False
    mapST[a] = b
    mapTS[b] = a
return True
rules: Check **both directions**. One map (s→t) lets `"badc" → "baba"` pass incorrectly because two different source chars collide onto the same target.
Enforce **consistency before overwriting**: if `a` already maps to something other than `b`, fail immediately.
Lengths must be equal first — `s.length() != t.length()` is an instant `false` (zip silently truncates, so guard it explicitly in Python).
Mapping is **positional**: the i-th char of s must map to the i-th char of t, every time it appears.
**O(1) space** is the honest claim — the alphabet is fixed (ASCII / Unicode-bounded), so the maps never exceed a constant.
whenToUse: Asked whether one sequence can be relabeled into another, preserving order and repetition
Structural / shape equality of two strings rather than literal equality
You see repeated characters that must always translate the same way
antiSignals: Only one-directional mapping is required → a single map suffices (rare; re-read the prompt)
Order does not matter, only multiset of chars → anagram / frequency count instead
Mapping can be many-to-one → it is not isomorphism, drop the reverse check
You need the actual mapping output, not a boolean → store and return the dict
remember.takeaway: Isomorphism = bijection = mapping consistent in both directions. The single most common bug is checking only s→t. Hold both maps and the problem collapses to a one-pass scan. The same two-map idea powers Word Pattern (LC 290) and any 'consistent relabeling' question.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you recognize that 'isomorphic' means a true bijection — not just that s maps to t, but that t maps back to s. The trap is settling for one hash map.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Using a single s→t map and forgetting the reverse, so `s = "badc", t = "baba"` wrongly returns true (both 'd' and 'c' would map to different chars, but two source chars are allowed to collide onto one target without the reverse check).
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State up front 'isomorphic means bijection, so I need consistency in both directions', then mention the index-encoding trick (first-occurrence positions) as an alternative one-array solution.

problemStatement:
Given two strings `s` and `t`, determine if they are **isomorphic**.

Two strings `s` and `t` are isomorphic if the characters in `s` can be replaced to get `t`.

All occurrences of a character must be replaced with another character while preserving the order of characters. ***No two characters may map to the same character***, but a character may map to itself.
constraints: s and t consist of any valid ASCII character
understanding: We need a one-to-one correspondence between the distinct characters of s and t such that replacing every char of s by its partner reproduces t exactly. 'One-to-one' is the crux: each s-char maps to exactly one t-char AND each t-char is the image of exactly one s-char. A char mapping to itself is fine.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are the strings guaranteed to be the same length?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, the constraints say t.length == s.length. Still, I'll guard it explicitly because in Python zip(s, t) silently stops at the shorter string and could hide a length mismatch.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can a character map to itself?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. 'a' → 'a' is allowed. The only forbidden thing is two distinct source chars mapping to the same target char, or one source char mapping to two different targets.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What character set — lowercase only, or full ASCII?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Full ASCII per the constraints. That keeps the space O(1) (bounded alphabet) but means I should use a general hash map, not a fixed 26-slot array, unless I size it for 128/256.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the empty string isomorphic to itself?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Length is ≥ 1 here, but conceptually two empty strings are trivially isomorphic — the loop body never runs and we return true.

examples.explanation: e→a, g→d. Both g's map to d consistently, and no two source chars share a target.
f→b, then o→a. The second o would need o→r, but o is already pinned to a. Inconsistent.
b→b, a→a, then d→b — but b is already the image of source char b. Two source chars (b and d) collide onto target b. The reverse map catches this.
p→t, a→i, e→l, r→e. Every char maps consistently both ways.

approaches.name: Two Hash Maps — Forward and Reverse (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The clean canonical answer. Lead with 'isomorphism is a bijection, so I track both directions'.
hints: What does 'isomorphic' actually require? Not just that every s-char picks a t-char, but that no two s-chars pick the SAME t-char. That second condition is the one a single map can't express.
Keep two maps: mapST records what each s-char must become, mapTS records which s-char each t-char came from. Walk both strings in lockstep.
For each pair (a, b): if a is already mapped and disagrees with b, fail; if b is already claimed by some other source char, fail; otherwise record both directions.
approaches.complexityReasoning: One pass over n characters, each doing O(1) average map operations → O(n) time. The maps hold at most one entry per distinct character of a bounded alphabet (≤ 128 ASCII) → O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
Walk `s` and `t` together, one index at a time. At position `i` we have a pair `(a, b) = (s[i], t[i])` and we must enforce that the pairing is consistent with everything seen so far — in **both** directions.

**Why two maps and not one.** A single `mapST` answers the question *"does `a` always become `b`?"* That catches `s = "foo", t = "bar"` because the second `o` would have to become `r` while `mapST[o]` is already `a`. But it does **not** catch the reverse failure. Consider `s = "badc", t = "baba"`. The forward map records `b→b`, `a→a`, then at the `d/b` pair it would happily add `d→b` — `d` has never been seen, so the forward check passes. The bug is that target `b` is now the image of *two* different source chars (`b` and `d`), which violates one-to-one. Only a reverse map `mapTS`, which already holds `b→b`, can reject `d` trying to claim `b`. This is the single most important insight in the problem: **isomorphism is a bijection, and a bijection needs both halves verified.**

**Why we check before we write.** At each step we first ask *"is `a` already mapped, and if so does it still agree?"* and *"is `b` already claimed by a different source?"* Only after both checks pass do we record `mapST[a] = b` and `mapTS[b] = a`. If we wrote first and checked later, the freshly written entry would always 'agree' with itself and the inconsistency would be masked — the same check-then-write discipline that the Two Sum hash map relies on.

**Why O(1) space is the honest claim.** The maps can never grow beyond the size of the alphabet. With ASCII that's at most 128 distinct keys in each map regardless of how long the strings are — a constant. So even though we allocate hash maps, the space is bounded by a constant, not by `n`. If an interviewer insists on calling it O(k) where k is the alphabet size, that's the same statement; the key point is it does not scale with input length.

**Why lengths must match first.** If `s` and `t` differ in length the strings cannot be isomorphic. In Java the loop bound makes this automatic only if you guard it; in Python `zip` truncates to the shorter string, so a length guard up front prevents `"ab"` and `"a"` from sneaking through.
approaches.insight: The mental model is a phone book that must work both forward and backward: given a name you find exactly one number, and given a number you find exactly one name. A one-to-one mapping is precisely a pair of lookups that never contradict each other. Whenever a prompt says 'no two X map to the same Y', that phrase is your cue to add the reverse map.

edgeCases.behavior: Single pair a/a, neither map seen, record a→a, loop ends → true (char maps to itself).
a→a recorded; then b/a: a is already claimed in mapTS by source a → reverse conflict → false.

pitfalls: Using only a forward s→t map — passes badc/baba incorrectly.
In Java, comparing Character objects with == can fail for values outside the cached range; use .equals or unbox to char as shown.
Writing the mapping before checking — masks the conflict because the entry agrees with itself.
Forgetting the length guard in Python — zip truncates and hides mismatched lengths.

approaches.name: Index Encoding — First-Occurrence Positions
approaches.whenToMention: A slick single-pass alternative when the interviewer asks 'can you avoid two maps?'. Shows mapping-pattern fluency.
hints: Two strings are isomorphic exactly when the PATTERN of first-occurrence positions is identical. "egg" → [0,1,1] (e first at 0, g first at 1, repeats 1). "add" → [0,1,1]. Same pattern → isomorphic.
For each index i, compare the index of the most recent previous occurrence of s[i] with that of t[i]. If they ever differ, the strings aren't isomorphic.
Store last-seen index per character in two arrays/maps. Two chars that 'first appear' at the same relative moment must continue to align.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Single pass, O(1) array updates per char → O(n) time. Two fixed-size last-index tables of 256 entries → O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
This approach reframes isomorphism as a **structural fingerprint**. Instead of tracking *which* character maps to which, we track *when each character last appeared*. Two strings are isomorphic if and only if, at every index `i`, the last-seen position of `s[i]` equals the last-seen position of `t[i]`.

**Why this works.** Encode each string as a sequence: at each position write down the index where the current character previously appeared (or a sentinel like 0 / "none" for a first appearance). For `"egg"` that sequence is `[none, none, 1]` — `e` is new, `g` is new, the second `g` last appeared at index 1. For `"add"` it is `[none, none, 1]` — identical. Two strings share the same fingerprint exactly when one can be relabeled into the other, because the fingerprint depends only on the *repetition structure*, not the actual letters. A bijection is precisely a relabeling that preserves repetition structure.

**Why it needs no reverse map.** The forward consistency and reverse consistency both fall out of comparing the *same* fingerprint for both strings simultaneously. If two source chars collided onto one target, their last-seen positions would diverge from the target's at the colliding index — the comparison catches it without an explicit second map. The two last-index tables are bookkeeping for a single comparison, not two independent mappings.

**Why it's a nice thing to mention.** It demonstrates you understand *what* isomorphism is at a structural level rather than mechanically applying two maps. In interviews, offering a second, conceptually different solution after the canonical one is a strong differentiator. The trade-off: it's slightly trickier to get the sentinel right (use 1-based indices or a clearly out-of-range marker so 'never seen' is distinguishable from 'seen at index 0').
approaches.insight: Isomorphism is invariance of repetition structure under relabeling. Encoding each string by 'where did this char last appear' projects away the actual letters and keeps only that structure — so equality of encodings IS isomorphism. This 'normalize to a canonical form, then compare' trick generalizes far beyond strings.

commonMistakes: Using a single s→t map and forgetting the reverse direction — passes badc/baba incorrectly.
Overwriting the mapping before checking consistency, masking the conflict.
Forgetting the length guard, especially in Python where zip truncates silently.
Comparing boxed Character with == in Java, which can fail outside the cached -128..127 range.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Only checking one direction
commonMistakesDetailed.why: A single s→t map allows two distinct source chars to map to the same target. On s="badc", t="baba", d→b is added without complaint because d was never seen, even though b is already a target.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Comparing boxed Characters with ==
commonMistakesDetailed.why: mapST.get(a) returns a Character object. Using != compares references, which only happens to work for cached values -128..127. For arbitrary chars it can give wrong answers. Unbox to char or use .equals.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
Character mapped = mapST.get(a);
if (mapped != b) return false;
commonMistakesDetailed.good: if (mapST.get(a) != null && mapST.get(a).charValue() != b) return false;

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Sentinel collision in index encoding
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If you store the raw index i and use 0 to mean 'unseen', a character genuinely first seen at index 0 is indistinguishable from one never seen. Store i+1.

followupVariations.hint: Same bijection idea, but between pattern characters and whole words. Split on spaces, then two maps.

followupVariations.title: Valid Anagram
followupVariations.hint: When order doesn't matter and only the multiset of chars counts — frequency map instead of bijection.

followupVariations.title: Group Anagrams
followupVariations.hint: Canonical-form trick: normalize each string to a key, then group — like the index-encoding fingerprint here.

followupVariations.title: Find and Replace Pattern
followupVariations.hint: Isomorphism applied to a list of words against one pattern — reuse the two-map check per word.

patternNote: Bijection via two hash maps. Recognise it whenever a prompt demands a consistent, one-to-one relabeling that preserves order — the giveaway phrase is 'no two characters may map to the same character'. The same forward+reverse discipline appears in Word Pattern and Find and Replace Pattern.
